# Mechanical artillery (torsion catapult, trebuchet) (`torsion_artillery_trebuchet`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by lever_mechanics_statics, crossbow_longbow, block_and_tackle
- Core idea: Greek and Roman catapults store energy in two tightly twisted bundles of sinew or hair rope, each with a wooden arm thrust through it; a slider, winch and trigger do the rest. All dimensions are multiples of the spring diameter, and Alexandrian engineers gave a formula for it from the weight of the shot. The trebuchet is simpler: a long beam on an axle with a sling on the long arm, pulled down on the short arm by a crew (traction) or by a box of several tonnes of earth or stone (counterweight). The counterweight machine throws 50 to 100 kg about 200 m and hits the same spot again and again, which is what breaks a wall.
- Pitfalls:
  - Drawing a medieval trebuchet for the Romans or a torsion catapult for the Middle Ages; the two belong to different eras
  - Leaving out the sling, which roughly doubles the range of a trebuchet
  - Sinew springs go slack when wet and must be re-tensioned evenly on both sides
  - Mechanical artillery kills defenders and smashes battlements; it rarely breaches a thick wall quickly
  - A fixed counterweight without wheels or a hinged box wastes much of its energy
- History: greece: 399 BC – catapults developed at Syracuse for Dionysius I; c. 350 BC – torsion springs (Macedon); c. 270 BC – calibration formula worked out at Alexandria; rome: 1st c. BC – scorpions and ballistae standard in Caesar's legions; 4th c. AD – one-armed onager; china: c. 4th c. BC – traction trebuchet described in the Mozi; 1272–1273 – counterweight trebuchets built by Muslim engineers break Xiangyang for the Mongols; islamic: 7th c. – traction trebuchets in the Arab conquests; c. 1187 – al-Tarsusi writes the first clear description of a counterweight trebuchet for Saladin; europe: late 6th c. – traction trebuchet reaches the Mediterranean with the Avars; 12th c. – counterweight trebuchet, origin (Byzantine or Islamic) disputed; still in use beside bombards in the 15th c.
- Read:
  - E. W. Marsden, Greek and Roman Artillery: Historical Development (1969)
  - Paul E. Chevedden, The Invention of the Counterweight Trebuchet: A Study in Cultural Diffusion, Dumbarton Oaks Papers 54 (2000)
  - Tracey Rihll, The Catapult: A History (2007)
